I have the honour to inform the house that a message has been received from the Senate informing this house that the Senate have adopted the following resolution:
Resolved: That pursuant to the provisions of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, the Senate of Canada hereby approves the purchase of the radio broadcasting stations and equipment of the Canadian National Railways by the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission for the sum of $50,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subsubtopic: CONDITION OP SETTLERS IN ROUYN AND OTHER PARTS OP QUEBEC
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) made reference to some settler in the Rouyn district of Quebec, who claimed to have been in very difficult circumstances and, I believe, was said to be in danger of starving to death, and I gathered from the observations made by the hon. member that this settler was induced to go on the land partly by this government, in conjunction with the province of Quebec and the municipalities. Reference was also made to other settlers. I have received to-day a telegram from Mr. J. E. Laforce, who acts for the Canadian National Railways on the committee with respect to this work. The telegram, if I may be permitted to read it, is as follows:
Relative statement the Gazette this morning. No families back to land were placed Rouyn or immediate surroundings. No back to land families province Quebec in distress provided they have shown willingness to work.
J. E. Laforce.
I then got the alphabetical list of the names and locations of all settlers in the territory of Abitibi and I do not find amongst them the name of the person who sent the telegram to the hon. member for Temiscouata. I also made inquiry faith respect to the placing of settlers in the Temiscouata constituency and I find that, as regards the settlers who were assisted by this government to locate there,
CMr. SauvA.l
we have only two and that they both signify to the committee that they are doing very well. I believe there are other settlers there who were placed by the province of Quebec, and of course I have no report upon their condition because that is a matter essentially for the province to deal with.

speechtext:
The hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) yesterday inquired concerning seed for soldier settlers. I asked him whether he would be good enough to let me have the name of the settler to whom he referred, and he did so. This settler is located not in the constituency of North Battleford but I believe in the constituency of Weyburn.
It would appear that the director of soldier settlement, in order to have the same treatment afforded to all settlers with respect to seed grain in the western provinces, in fact throughout Canada wherever the need arose, made it possible for all settlers to be treated alike. They could apply to the municipality, the same as the civilian settler or any other farmer, and the director, acting within the scope of his authority, gave them a preferential lien, withdrawing the preferred position of the crown, as it were, with respect to seed.
The settler to whom the hon. member for North Battleford made reference received seed last year and was advised some months ago of the course he should pursue if he were without sufficient seed for this season's operation. It would appear that he has ample seed to take care of the land that belongs to the crown in the right of the dominion, but that he has purchased other lands, to take care of which he may not have seed enough. The position was indicated to him some time ago and if he will follow the procedure as outlined, he should have no difficulty.

The house resumed from Thursday, April 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific Railway system and for other purposes-Mr. Manion.-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

Before we take up any
of the sections which were allowed to stand, we might first dispose of the question of amalgamation. It is the intention of the government to put in a clause as part IV of the bill. It was thought that by doing this the

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
clause would stand out more plainly as referring to the whole bill. I have given copies of the proposed amendment to my right hon. friend and other hon. members opposite. If it is agreeable to the committee this clause will be put in as part IV and numbered section 27, or possibly some other number if the numbering of the sections is changed. The amendment reads:
Nothing in this act shall be deemed to authorize the amalgamation of any railway company which is comprised in the National Railways with any railway company which is comprised in Pacific railways nor to authorize the unified management and control of the railway system which forms part of National railways with the railway system which forms part of Pacific railways.
I might say that this amendment has been submitted to the legal officers of the department as well as to the legal officers of the Department of Justice. It is thought that this amendment will provide against any amalgamation of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways.

As I
understand the amendment, its purport is t a prevent the taking over by the Canadian Pacific of any branch lines from the Canadian National, or visa versa. I do not think it was ever intended that such an amendment should go that far. I may be wrong, as one cannot follow the ramifications of an amendment of this character simply by hearing it read.

This is to preclude the
amalgamation of the two companies but there is nothing to prevent the establishing of joint running rights, the joint use of terminals, the linking up of telegraph or ticket offices and so on.

At the time the minister mentioned his intended amendment to the committee I suggested for his consideration the adding to the section of certain words which now appear elsewhere in the act. These were, "in so far as the provisions of this act may be inconsistent with the provisions of this section, they shall be read in the light thereof and be so construed as to conform therewith." Either the minister or the Prime Minister stated that the addition of such words would be superfluous as their intent would be covered by the section as worded. If that is so, I will not press the matter any further.

I think the right hon
gentleman is referring to section 24, which still stands, and which reads:
In the event of any conflict between an order of the Board of Railway Commissioners and that of any tribunal, the order or decision of the tribunal shall prevail.

No, it was
with reference to amalgamation, that the provisions of this act shall be read in the light of the section it is now being proposed to insert, and that nothing therein shall further amalgamation.

The reason we have made this section a separate and distinct part is to cover that very point. It was thought that by making it a separate part it would stand out more emphatically. It could have been put in as one of the preliminary clauses which apply to the whole bill, but I am advised by the legal fraternity that making it a distinct part would make the right hon. gentleman's recommendation unnecessary.

I suppose the minister is
prepared to admit that the same authority that inserts this amendment can. strike it out?
Of course. We cannotbind any future parliament and when my' hon. friend is Prime Minister he may change-this bill or do anything he wishes.
I hope the amendment will! come in long before I am Prime Minister^
Does the minister really think that this amendment is of any real value; does he think there are any teeth in it?

The amendment is made
to meet the wishes of -hon. friends opposite Who apparently thought they saw a coloured gentleman in the woodpile. As the hon. member for Cartier said in his speech, he thought this was going to lead to amalgamation. The government had no thought of amalgamation but in order to cooperate with hon. friends opposite, this clause has been suggested. If they desire that it should not be included in the hill, I do not think it would change the effect of the bill at all. It was to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite as well as those outside the house who might think that there was something wrong with the bill that this amendment was suggested.

In, other words, it is merely
an expression of intention or hope?
The intention, and I think the effect of this amendment is to prevent the amalgamation of the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways.

I am not going to argue at any great length with respect to this provision, because the government and the minister have been good enough to accept the suggestion from this side of the house, but I want to put myself on record so that there may
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

be no comeback so far as I am concerned that this is merely a pious hope-and apparently it is about the only thing we can get- that is placed in the bill stating that there shall be no amalgamation. I want to point out to the minister once more that this bill which we are discussing provides for amalgamation of the railroads of Canada; despite anything that may be included in the bill, its actual operation is amalgamation.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); Nonsense.
My hon. friend from York-Sunbury is the best judge of nonsense of any man in the house.
I am, and I am looking right at the hon. member.
Since I have been in the house I have never heard the hon. member give expression to anything but nonsense of the worst kind.
Oh, oh.
Do not any of you Tories think you are going to get away with this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member address the chair?
Will the chairman keep his own side in order? I do not want these men who do not know what they are talking about to interfere in my discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must address the chair.

I am addressing the chair now. I do not intend to allow the Tory party to give away the Canadian National without the people of this country knowing what they are doing. The bill itself provides for the amalgamation of our Canadian railroads. I believe the minister is sincere in thinking that this amendment is of value. I think it is of value to this extent only that the government is enunciating in this provision that it does not intend the amalgamation of the railroads of Canada, but that does not detract in the slightest from this bill which provides for running rights of one road over the other, the merging of services and all the ramifications that go into the operation of a railway. The amalgamation of the railroads of Canada is right in this bill.
That is just your opinion.

If I were as ignorant as my hon. friend, I would not give expression to such ignorance.
tMr. Heenan.]
If the hon. member knew anything about the English language, he would not make such a statement.
If I were as ignorant as my hon. friend, I would go to law school.
If the hon. member lived in the days of Parnell, he would be a dynamiter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to address the chair.
All I am asking you, sir, to do, is to keep order on both sides.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what I am trying to do.

I just want to give warning that neither the chairman nor anyone else will shut me up on this measure, because when it means putting 20,000 or 30,000 workers on the streets in order to help the moneylenders of New York, I am going to fight for the citizens of Canada.
I am not going to argue against this amendment, but I want to put myself on record. I am going to support it because it seems to be a pious hope the government have that the railroads will not be amalgamated, but I cannot accept it as being of value and I may be all wrong-
, Mr. MANION:	The hon. member is.

but I want to tell the government and the minister they are all wrong on it. Every provision in this bill means the amalgamation of the operations of the railroads of Canada. Apart from that I want to say that I am prepared to accept the amendment.
I have in my constituency as many and probably more railwavmen than has the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in his.
Why does the hon. member not fight for them?

I have
just as much interest in them as he has in his, but I am not a self-constituted champion as he is.
I know the hon. member is not.

The only position the railroad men in my constituency take is that the principle of amalgamation shall not be included in this bill. It is not included in the bill, but to make assurance doubly sure and to relieve the minds of the

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
railwaymen of this country the government has inserted an amendment which has been read to the committee to-day. If the hon. gentleman knew anything about the drawing and construction of statutes, he would know it is not necessary to insert in a bill a provision which negatives something which does not exist. This proposed amendment is in law absolutely unnecessary, but in order to satisfy public opinion and especially that which I have the honour to represent directly, namely, the railwaymen in my constituency, this is being put into the bill; they are quite satisfied with it and I venture to say that not one of them is asking the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to champion their cause in the house.
Could the minister inform the committee whether there is at present any move on foot to amalgamate the services of the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National express companies?

I am afraid I cannot answer definitely as to that. I may say quite frankly that certain cooperative measures are being studied by the management of the two railways and, generally speaking, the government does not hear the result of such detailed studies until something definite has developed from them. I understand there have been discussions as to operating the express companies to a greater extent in cooperation than has been the case in the past, but further than that I am sorry I cannot definitely inform my hon. friend.

I happen to have in my possession a communication addressed to me just a few days ago dealing with this question. While the talk is of cooperation and consolidation, this letter refers distinctly to amalgamation of the two companies with the primary intention of saving large sums of money and of course with the result of letting out large numbers of employees. In this communication which comes from a reputable source-and although it is confidential, I will let the minister see portions of it-they talk of the amalgamation of the two services. They claim that the Canadian National service is much superior to that of .the Canadian Pacific, and they believe the best portions of the business of the Canadian National will be picked up and amalgamated with the Canadian Pacific. AVhether that be correct or not, I cannot say, but the impression is at present gaining ground throughout the country that the privately owned company is taking off the best portions of the Canadian National railway system and
that is being amalgamated, while the government or the country will be left with the worst portions of the Canadian National railway services and will no doubt have to maintain that as a losing proposition as time goes on. That is likely to happen. We have already had the consolidation of services between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto and this was one of the best services which the Canadian National had so far as passenger traffic was concerned. If that is going to be the basis of cooperation between the two railways, I am afraid we are going to do something which we shall ultimately regret. The information contained in this letter, coming from what I believe is a reputable source, is that the income of the Canadian National Express Company is claimed to be much higher than that of the Canadian Pacific Express Company, and if we are going to have instance after instance of .the best paying services of the Canadian National system being amalgamated with the poor services of the Canadian Pacific, I am afraid this bill is hardly worth the time we are giving to it in the house.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has any right to imply that we are going to have instance after instance of the Canadian National being sacrificed to the interests of Canadian Pacific. I have not yet heard of anything which would justify such an assertion. I am just as interested in the Canadian National as is my hon. friend. Furthermore, if as he suggests the managing officers of the Canadian National Railways were so stupid as to permit the Canadian Pacific Railway to pick off their plums in that fashion, then I think the sooner we got rid of the whole outfit the better. That would be my feeling about it. But I do not believe that the managing officers of the Canadian National are stupid. I believe that they are just as capable of taking care of themselves as are the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I believe that they will take care of themselves in any cooperative measures that may be adopted.
My hon. friend said something about the Canadian National giving up its service between Ottawa and Toronto, but the Canadian Pacific has also given up its service between Montreal and Toronto. That is part of the cooperative measures that they are working out. Though on the surface the Canadian National so far as the service between Ottawa and Toronto is concerned apparently suffers, my understanding is that under these pooling arrangements the earnings are divided so that there would not actually be any loss;

and as between Toronto and Montreal it is the Canadian Pacific that gives up its service and the Canadian National runs its trains. But it is on the basis of a fifty-fifty division of doing away with services and a fifty-fifty division of the profits accruing from that curtailment of operations. My hon. friend is usually fair, but I do not think he is fair in suggesting that the Canadian National Railways will permit the Canadian Pacific Railway to take over any portion of their better paying services unless the Canadian National gets an equally valuable quid pro quo. I am confident of that. The officers of the Canadian National are experiencing no interference by the government in any shape or form in regard to these cooperative measures, and I repeat, that if they are stupid enough to let the Canadian Pacific Railway put it over them they are too stupid to run a railway anyway.
I may say that that impression is gaining ground among a great many people.
It is not very complimentary to the management.
I will read one or two lines from these communications which I have here and which I believe come from a very reliable source.
If the hon. gentleman is going to read communications to the house it is only fair that he should say from whom they come. Otherwise I submit that he has no right to read them.

I have not read any portion of these communications for that very reason, but I have what I think are official figures showing the business of the Canadian National express and of the Canadian Pacific express, which services I claim are likely to be amalgamated or coordinated in the very near future. According to my information the business of the Canadian National express was $594,000 as compared with $216,000 for the Canadian Pacific express, so if there is going to be an amalgamation on a fifty-fifty basis we can understand how unfair it would be in that case to the Canadian National railway system.

I did not say that there
was to be an amalgamation on a fifty-fifty basis, but that whatever cooperative measures were put into effect, the doing away of trains and services, and1 the remuneration, would be on a fifty-fifty basis.

I bring this matter to the
attention of the minister and the house because I have received a lot of letters from 
different parts of the country along this very same line. But if we have the assurance of the minister that any cooperation or amalgamation of services, although I am opposed to the whole thing, will be done on a fair basis, I have no more to say.

The hon. gentleman may
have my assurance so far as the matter is within my control. I would object with all the power I possessed against the Canadian National giving to the Canadian Pacific something that it did not get a return for- absolutely.

Under this bill we are
appointing a chairman and a board of trustees for a period of years. They cannot be removed by the minister or by this house without the concurrence of the upper house. Am I right in that?
By parliament; that is right.

Then in Part II of the bill we are giving the chairman of the board of trustees all the power that it is possible to give to any trustee. We are giving him power to amalgamate traffic and amalgamate terminals. The minister will not deny that.
I do not admit that joint operation means amalgamation at all.

It means an amalgamation of services if it means anything at all. We appoint this board of trustees, and this government has no control over the board. This house cannot dismiss the chairman of the board of trustees without the concurrence of the upper house. The two .houses of parliament have to concur in a resolution before he can be dismissed. If this house passed a resolution to dismiss the chairman of the board of trustees, and the upper house refused to concur in it, the chairman would remain in his office. Now, suppose that the chairman of the board of trustees under the power given him in Part II of this bill does things which he is empowered to do, and which mean the amalgamation of service; what effect will this amendment which the minister proposes have? I cannot see that it will have any

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
effect in preventing the amalgamation of services. May I say this, that a railroad is really a service that is given to the people, and if you are going to permit the amalgamation of services, I do not see how you can get away from amalgamating the railways. Suppose that the board of trustees sanctions the amalgamation of terminals, the amalgamation of railway ticket offices, and of stations, and so forth, I do not see how by this amendment we can undo what they have done in the wray of amalgamation. What effect would the amendment have? I am asking for information. The chairman of the board of trustees is appointed for a period of seven years, and he cannot be dismissed except by a resolution passed by both houses of parliament, and if in the meantime he goes on amalgamating terminals and ticket offices and services and stations, there will be very little left of the Canadian National Railways at the end of seven years.

I do not agree at all with the hon. gentleman in regard to that. I submit that at the end of seven years, if we get the right kind of trustee, as we hope to do, we shall have the same condition on the Canadian National as we have on the Canadian Pacific so far as independent operation is concerned. It is true that some of the divisional points and some of the branch lines may be worked jointly, and it would have been a good thing for this country had that been done many years ago. There are two things which my hon. friend seems to forget in his remarks. In the first place, we are appointing trustees whose duty it will be to look after the interests of the Canadian National Railways. We are not appointing trustees to work for the Canadian Pacific Railway. If we should be so unlucky as to get a chairman of trustees who would betray his trust, I have no doubt whatsoever that this house would dismiss him at the next session and that the action of this house would be endorsed by the Senate, because after all the Senate, without a doubt, represents the best thought in this country just as does this House of Commons, and if some trustee should be false to his trust I cannot conceive of the other chamber in justice and decency not taking action to protect the Canadian National Railways, just the same as we would. To assume what my hon. friend suggests, we must first of all assume that the trustees are to be false to their trust, and secondly that the other chamber is also to be false to its trust. That would be a wrong assumption. I do not believe that at the end of seven years, if these cooperative measures last so long,
there will be any difference except that there will be some joint operation here and there which should exist, because as was pointed out in a committee this morning, and as I have pointed out on the floor of this house, there are many opportunities for joint operation of ticket offices, for instance, and telegraph offices on expensive comers. Joint operation of such services could only redound to the benefit and profit of the two railways, and it could not in any way take away from the independence and autonomy of the Canadian National Railways.

While I was relieved to hear the statement of the Minister of Railways on the matter raised by the hon. member for North Winnipeg a few moments ago, I feel that he should be made aware of the fact that there is now growing over those sections of the line where there are pooled services in central Canada-I refer to the Ottawa-Toronto, Montreal-Toronto, and Ottawa-Montreal pooled services-a feeling that there is something wrong. The remark made by the minister to-day may dissipate that feeling. But when travelling on the train the other day one of the old conductors who-has been employed in the service for about twenty-four years, evidently a very estimable type, and well educated, informed me that there had been a sudden transfer of sales of passenger tickets to the extent of nearly eighty-seven per cent in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Between here and Toronto?

Between Montreal and Toronto. He expressed grave concern about the situation, discussed the matter at some length with me, and asked me what the terms of pooling were to be. I said I did not know, but that the matter could be taken up, and that I would ask the minister. I am now asking who determines the terms of pooling? Is it the minister, the board of trustees or the tribunal? Secondly, what principle of pooling would the minister suggest, and thirdly is the principle of pooling adopted to be established as a regulation which the tribunal or trustees must follow. For example, in addition to the point raised by the hon. member for North Winnipeg, I would suggest this to the minister: Where in the past railway points having both lines operating through them showed forty per cent to the Canadian Pacific Railway and sixty per cent to the Canadian National Railways, and where it is found that those figures are suddenly switched around under the pooling arrangements to sixty-five per cent to the
[DOT]1332
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

Canadian Pacific Railway and the balance to the Canadian National Railways, what basis would be followed? If disputes, in regard to terms of pooling are to be left to the decision of the tribunal, how are we to approach the tribunal? Reading the second to last clause in the bill I find the following:
Save as provided by this section no order, decision or proceeding of a tribunal shall be questioned or reviewed, restrained or removed by any process whatever in or to any court.
I do not know whether in that section the House of Commons is included.
Read the other parts of the section.
I should like the minister to cover those points, if possible, because a good deal of disturbance has been created.

I am afraid the hon. member has covered a lot of ground in only a few questions, and possibly I may not be able to answer him fully; however I shall try. In the first place, in regard to tickets being sold between Montreal and Toronto-I believe that is the section of the road he indicated-and the suggestion that a larger proportion of passenger traffic tickets were being sold through offices of the Canadian Pacific, I would answer as follows: In the first place, I do not think that is a correct statement, because there would be no advantage in buying from one ticket office rather than the other for the simple reason that the earnings of the pooled trains are divided fifty-fifty between the two systems.
The conductor would have no object in misinforming me.
He probably misinformed himself.
He ought to know, he would collect the tickets.

But not the money. The money goes to the railways; the tickets go to the conductors. I believe I am correctly informed when I say that the railways have pooled their passenger traffic between Ottawa and Toronto and between Montreal and Toronto. Between Ottawa and Toronto the Canadian Pacific handles the train. So that as the hon. member for Melville mentioned the other evening, those people who have been accustomed to travelling to intermediate points between here and Toronto by way of the Canadian National railway will find that the service was not as good as it was previ-
ously, because the Canadian Pacific is carrying on a joint service between those two points. The same is true, on the other hand, with regard to the service between Montreal and Toronto. No doubt there will be a greater volume of traffic on that service than between Ottawa and Toronto. In that case, the service is pooled and carried by the Canadian National Railways.
I was not going to waste the time of the committee by giving illustrations to show how difficult it is for one railway to obtain an advantage over the other. However, I believe I should tell one incident which occurred and about which I happened to know. The Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National were both running their sixty-miles-an-hour fast trains between Montreal and Toronto. While both railways were carrying a great many passengers, it was decided the two fast trains were not required, and that one could carry the business. They thought, as I believe, that the change was to the advantage of both railroads. The Canadian Pacific agreed that the Canadian National should handle the fast train service between Montreal and Toronto but since the Windsor station was in a better location than the Bonaventure station, that the trains should run out of and into the Windsor station, despite the fact that a Canadian National train was being used. So far as returns were concerned, it would not have meant one dollar's difference t'o the Canadian National. But the directors and management of the national system took the attitude that if the train ran both out of and into the Windsor station damage would be done to the prestige of the national system and that there would be a loss from the standpoint of advertising. After a good deal of wrangling it has been decided that the train shall go out of the Windsor station to Toronto, but shall enter the Bonaventure station upon its return to Montreal. I believe this illustration goes to show how anxious the management and directors of the Canadian National have been to secure a fair deal for the national system. While the Canadian Pacific argued that the Windsor station should be used exclusively- and I believe their argument carried some weight-the management and directors of the national system insisted that that should not be the case.
I believe this illustration goes to show that officials of the Canadian National system have no intention of giving up any rights, prestige or advertising value connected with any service it now possesses. So far as tickets are concerned, I repeat that the returns from the pooled services are divided equally between

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
the two railway systems. If the hon. member cared to walk over to the station he would see a notice containing the words "pooled train tickets for sale here." The returns on those tickets are divided.

They are
divided on what basis?

So far as I know, on a
fifty-fifty basis.

How can
justice be maintained by dividing on a fifty fifty basis? If one system had been selling sixty per cent of the tickets between Montreal and Toronto and the other system selling only forty per cent, a fifty-fifty division would not be fair.

But from other points
probably the reverse percentage would be the case. If the hon. member will look over the passenger statistics I believe he will find that on the whole, the Canadian Pacific has been doing a better paying passenger business than has the Canadian National, for the simple reason that the Pacific system has as feeders a trans-Atlantic steamship service, and a transpacific steamship service. , For those reasons they get a great deal of transcontinental or long haul traffic. My information is that they have thus been getting a larger average revenue per passenger carried than has the Canadian National. Therefore I believe that if passenger service returns are split fifty-fifty the Canadian National system would be getting a fair deal all round. While I may not be able to go into the details as to former percentages of traffic now pooled I believe if both railways can make big savings by cutting off unnecessary trains, they are thereby gaining so much that the possible small amount which one might have gained here or another might have gained there might easily be forgotten.

If I heard that the Canadian National was getting an unfair deal I should certainly make inquiry as to how such a matter arose. After this bill passes, suppose there is amalgamation of services at a given point and it is apparent that the Canadian National railway is getting unfair treatment. The only power the minister has would be the same power as my hon. friend has or any member of this house. When moneys are required by the Canadian National-
Only capital expenditures.

No, deficits, interest on bonds, practically everything except operating details has to be passed by this house. I believe the minister is
sincere in that, but I want to point out something. In reply to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) the minister said that if it were discovered .that these trustees, although appointed for seven years, and not subject to dismissal except on an address from both houses of parliament, were betraying-probably that word is too strong, but were making errors that favoured the Canadian Pacific-means could be taken to dispense with their services. But I want the minister to look at this from my viewpoint for a moment, I think this will drive home the argument that I have been attempting to make for some days. Suppose under this measure the two railroad companies get together-I will admit it would probably have been better, as the minister says, if they had done it many years ago, but they did not. But now they get together. Take, for example, Winnipeg; there are four yards there; Fort Rouge, the Canadian Pacific yard, the Canadian Pacific new yard at North Trans-cona, and the Canadian National yard at South Transcona. Suppose they merge these four yards into one. They construct rails to 
radiate from that yard. It would probably [DOT]cost thousands and thousands of dollars to do that. After that is done, that money spent, the other employees are gone. Dismissal of trustees would not alter that in the least. There is unquestionably a deliberate attempt being made right across this country, by such statements as have been put into the hands of my hon. friend and which have been read in good faith, to convey the impression that this measure that is being passed in an effort to rescue the railways from their present situation, and particularly the Canadian National Railways, is designed to scuttle the Canadian National in the interests of the Canadian Pacific. May I suggest with all respect to those who want to talk further on this matter that we accept the amendment now, lest peradventure we lose it with all that may be in it. I can imagine myself in the minister's chair, exclaiming, "Well, if they don't want to have it I will withdraw it." Let us have it by all means.

In our section of the country we are quite willing to cooperate, but apparently cooperation means elimination or extermination. I said, when the first reading of the bill was under consideration, that so far as the railway commissioners were concerned the port of the country from which I come had never received fair treatment from
them. To substantiate this statement, I will say-and the house will be surprised to learn this-that the Duff commission never found it possible to devote so much as half an hour of their time to a consideration of the problems of that section of the country right on the ground itself. They never visited any section of the Transcontinental line passing through that part of Canada. In a word, the Duff commission did not think it desirable to visit a section of the Canadian National Railways comprising one-third of the whole system, and on that ground alone we feel that we have a grievance-a grievance which it is hard for us to understand at all. Time was not a matter of great concern to the commission, so that there is no excuse from that point of view. I contend that they should have been on the ground to see for themselves the physical situation of the railways.
I wish to bring up to-day a matter which is of interest to the whole of Canada; I refer to the passenger and freight service of the railways from coast to coast. A little over a year ago the national trains were taken off from Montreal to North Bay and Cochrane and from Cochrane to Winnipeg; for what reason we do not know. No one in Canada, certainly no one in that part of the country, can imagine what could have induced them to take this step. We find on the other hand that trains were put on in sections where there is no population nor any local traffic. On the longest section of the run from Halifax to Quebec and on to Winnipeg and through to the Pacific coast trains were taken off. The suggestion was made that the reason might be that the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway was charging too much for trains using its roadbed. So far that suggestion has not been verified but there is no doubt that trains were taken off in that northern section.
I repeat, we are willing to cooperate and to do everything we possibly can to make the Canadian National Railways a going concern, but it seems to us that passenger service is being taken away from the Canadian National system and handed over to the Canadian Pacific. At the present time trains leaving Quebec pass through Montreal to Ottawa and then go on to North Bay, whereas in the past they went directly from Quebec to Cochrane and on to Winnipeg. A similar situation exists in the maritimes. The committee will understand to what extent the Canadian National system has been the loser during the past year and a half so far as passenger service is concerned. People travelling from our section

I believe, as I have said both privately and publicly, that the Minister of Railways has the welfare of the Canadian National system at heart, but no matter what he says in answer to the criticism of Mr. Deachman, the fact remains that to-day the Canadian National Railways are losing passenger and freight service, and this applies more particularly to my own section of the country. Before the Christmas recess I asked the minister what seemed to me a perfectly reasonable question but one that apparently came to him as a great surprise, namely, when the passenger service would be really established over the National Transcontinental line, and he told me it was not within his province to know when that would take place. Surely the Minister of Railways, who is in charge of the department, should know what is taking place in that section of the country, a section which, as I have said, constitutes one-third of the Canadian National system. Only a few months ago I listened with surprise to a statement made by the Prime Minister to the effect that it was practically a blunder to have built a railway linking up east and west in the northern sections of Canada. I am not a lawyer and I

The point I am making is that they are protected under this new bill just as they were under the old act. In other words, in the new bill there is the statement that that part of section 179 of the Railway Act which relates to compensation to employees for financial loss is incorporated in the bill. I do not wish to go further than that. So far as we have gone in the bill, I am quite agreeable, but I do not wish to carry it further than that. Of course I will promise to consider anything, but there is no use of pretending to the hon. member that I am going to do something which I do not intend to do. I do not believe there is any likelihood of putting in the bill the provision he suggests.

I know the towns of Sioux Lookout and Rainy River as well as does the hon. member, because we both come from that section of the country. As a matter of fact I do not believe there is any likelihood of either point being abandoned. But should they be abandoned I submit under the act the men will be protected, and I think the hon. member agrees with that statement. At any rate I submit that is so because section 179 distinctly states that in case Of abandoning a station or divisional point or creating a new divisional point thei men will he compensated. So in case of an abandonment the men will be compensated by virture of that amendment.
If I understood the hon. member correctly he wishes to go further and say that if in this divisional point men should lose their positions they should be compensated because of loss of employment. We could not have a law to look after employees at Sioux Lookout and Rainy River and not have a law to look after employees at Winnipeg and Port Arthur. I have said that the hon. member's suggestion is similar to that made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg. I do not believe in promising what I do not intend1 to do.

There is no use promising something which I cannot carry out.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has placed himself on record as wishing to go farther than the legislation provides. I appeal to him to let the bill go through as it is.
I suppose it is an Irishman's privilege to keep on talking until he is understood.
There are two Irishmen here.

I point out to the minister that I was not asking for a special consideration for employees at Rainy River or Sioux Lookout, but was merely stating their ease as an example. I should hope the measure I suggest would apply to all railroad employees in Canada. Again I point out that my proposal was entirely different from that moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg. The hon. member asked for compensation for all those who lost their positions. I am asking not only for compensation for loss of positions, but I am asking this: If a railroad company abandons a station because of the merging of services, and some of the men who are not required are dismissed, then we should compensate those people for loss of residence. They axe as much entitled to compensation as those who are transferred to another point. Let me give the example again. Supposing the Canadian Pacific wanted to change their terminal from Ottawa to a point five or six miles out. Under the act they compensate me for the loss of my property rights, so that employees may go and build a home at the other terminal point. That is what is contemplated under section 179. But under the new bill the Canadian Pacific Railway may abandon Ottawa entirely. Under the present regulations the railway companies and the men will get together to negotiate how many men in Ottawa are entitled to move to another point to secure work. In those circumstances the men transferred will come under section 179 of the Railway Act and receive compensation for loss of property. But if half a dozen men owning property in Ottawa are dismissed because of this economy I suggest they are entitled to compensation for loss of property. I do not wish to delay the committee, but I should like the minister to take this matter into consideration.. I suggest to the minister that instead of accepting or rejecting the amendment now before us he just insert the words "under section 179 of the Railway Act."

The minister said a
few moments ago that he had discussed with various officers concerned, the matter o>f embodying in this bill the whole of section 179 of the Railway Act. A number of hon. members are very much interested in that point, quite apart from the protection it will afford the employees from a financial point of view. It will be recognized by the minister and by the committee, I believe, that in the case of an abandonment of a terminal point, people other than employees are, in a financial sense, vitally interested. I can perhaps do no better than give a concrete illustration of just what can happen under such circumstances. This particular case, although relating to a comparatively small point, was pretty well advertised at the time, it may be in the recollection of the minister although he was not minister then. In my riding at that time, although not now, was a small divisional point, termed Big Valley. It was largely a railway point, depending almost entirely on the fact that it was a terminal point. Based upon the fact that a large proportion of the population were railway men the village erected a fair sized schoolhouse, sold debentures and generally obligated itself for a very large sum considering its population, in order to take care of the railway men's families. When a point of that character is abandoned, a small point where a large proportion of the inhabitants were railway men and their families, they of course suffer very severely. Many of their houses are standing abandoned, some were purchased for a song by the farmers and hauled out on the farms thereabouts. They lost all value in fact. The men suffered severe financial loss, and I am in full sympathy with what has been said with respect to protecting those men. But I understand they were protected by the particular provision in the act referred to, whatever that protection is worth.
As far as they were concerned.

Yes, they have been
dealt with as far as that section goes. But I want to point out to the minister and to the committee that no protection is provided in this bill-in fact protection is precluded by the fact that part of the section only is referred to-no protection is provided for the village itself and others who suffer, although not employees. Under the entire section 179

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
such people were given some slight protection; at least to this extent, that they did receive notice and were entitled to lay their case before the railways and before the railway commission before the transfer took place, and to endeavour at least to get some recompense. I think it will be recognized by every one that under those circumstances, where a small community has erected public utilities, schoolhouses and so on far beyond its normal needs and sold debentures based on the railway property and the railway men as taxpayers, and then those men are removed because of a change of policy on the part of the railway, the village itself and the rest of the inhabitants suffer almost as much as the railway men, and by this bill no protection whatever is given them. I am not going to labour that point, but I had hoped that when the question arose as to reference being made to the entire section, that point of view would have been given consideration, and those interested, the municipal authorities and others, given notice of the contemplated action and a right to appear and lay their case before the board with the possibility of receiving compensation.
As I recollect, neither the men nor the village in this case received any compensation. There seemed to be some loophole, through the abandonment -not being an entire abandonment. The abandonment was practically speaking complete, but some half dozen men or less were left with a caretaker's job, and technically the abandonment had not taken place although in actual effect it had. The place is not in my riding, and the matter has not been brought to my attention for some years, but as I remember it, not one dollar of compensation was received by the men or the municipality. But the section did contemplate that protection should be given, and under this bill; by the reference being limited to that part of section 179 which deals only with compensation to the -men, any possibility of compensation being awarded to or representations heard from the municipal authorities and others affected is completely eliminated. I recognize of course that the mere fact that section 179 is not specifically referred to does not necessarily mean that it will not govern, it simply says that the act will prevail over all inconsistent provisions with the exception of certain specified sections. If that part of section 179 proves to be inconsistent that part would still prevail. It does not say that the rest of section 179 will necessarily be inconsistent, but by the fact that one part is picked out and referred to and provision made that even if it prove
inconsistent it will still prevail, I think we may fairly take it for granted that the balance that is not referred to will be considered as inconsistent and so will be eliminated. I do not know whether that particular aspect, and the conditions I have referred to and the position of others than employees has been given consideration. If not I do hope the minister even at this late hour will consider that viewpoint and will see to it by the inclusion of the entire section if possible that this amount of reasonable protection will be afforded to those interested.

I happen to know the Big Valley case, and I am free to say it was not a satisfactory decision. The finding of fact by the railway board was that the divisional point at Big Valley had not 'been abandoned, and therefore the section did not take effect. Subsequently the railway employees strove to get an amendment to section 179, I think it was at the last session, to cover such a case. That amendment was refused. But my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) is a little in error I think in his construction of section 179. I know of nothing in the section as it now stands that enables any compensation to be paid to other than employees. It is simply protection for employees. The Big Valley case was heard in the west, and doubtless the municipal authorities of Big Valley itself appeared and made representations.
That is what I said, it at least gave them notice, and opportunity to be heard.

There will be no difference under this proposed act. The railway board could either hold its sessions in private, or could give notice and let representations be made by the municipality; there is no change in this bill in that regard, so that whatever benefit there may have been in the forepart of section 179 is not interfered with by the present bill.
In regard to the section the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) dealt with, complaint is made that by pooling services between, say, Toronto and Montreal, some men are left without work. That pooling has not taken place under this bill. It might have taken place any time within the last fifteen or twenty years. It would be governed, if at all, by section 179 of the Railway Act. Pooling may take place under this bill, but only by arrangement, such as can be made now. My friend wants to amend section 179. I submit his proposition is not

in order at this time, because we are not discussing the Railway Act. If he seeks to amend section 179 by including in it some provision that every man who is deprived of work through an arrangement between the railways is to be given some sort of compensation, that is a very drastic change. Without seeking to stop my hon. friend-it would be rather late to stop him-I think his amendment deals with a matter that is not before the committee. His speech in terms suggested that the minister consider an amendment to the Railway Act. The minister says he will, but it has nothing to do with what we are now discussing.

The hon. member seems to be familiar with the Railway Act. May I ask him whether under the new system authorization will be given to abandon any divisional point or junction at the sweet will of those who may have charge of the matter, as happened at Matapedia in my own corn stituency, which had been a divisional point for forty years, connecting Gaspe with the Intercolonial. The change was made overnight from Matapedia to Campbellton, New Brunswick, in another province. The railway leaving Gaspe runs two hundred miles to Matapedia, and that has been the divisional point for the last forty years. Now the Canadian National has shifted the terminus from that point to Campbellton, thirteen miles away, involving the dismissal of all officials, because they say it is cheaper for them to go to Campbellton than to keep the terminus at Matapedia.
Has that been done?
Yes.
But not under the proposed act.	[DOT]

No, but I am asking whether there will be any change in this regard. Matapedia was the terminal point fixed by the Quebec legislature when it incorporated the road. At that time it gave subsidies, fixing the terminal there, and now it has been removed to another province, adding thirteen miles to the run. Surely that is ridiculous. A man reaches Matapedia and he has to go on to Campbellton and then come back to Matapedia on his way to Montreal. Is there any sense in that?

speechtext: As I understand the point of order raised by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), the case cited by the hon. member for Bonaventure would not fall under the amendment which is being considered and which deals only with employees. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) brought up a question which has been answered by one of my hon. friends from Toronto. I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman something that he has forgotten. At the previous sitting of the committee an amendment was moved to section 16 under part II of the bill dealing with cooperation. The amendment was as follows:
Where the execution or carrying out of such a measure, plan or arrangement involves the doing of any act which by any statute requires the leave, sanction, assent or approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, no such measure, plan or arrangement shall be effective without the approval of the said board.
So that we made it absolutely subject to the approval of the board, where it would have been in the ordinary course of events so subject. So far as the rest of the act is concerned, it is in the same position as before.
Has the matter to which I have referred been brought to the attention of the minister? I refer to the moving of the terminus from Matapedia to Campbellton. It is a grave injustice.

I do not remember who
drew it to my attention but someone did because I am familiar with it. The matter is entirely in the hands of the management, and if they were required to go before the board I presume they did. At any rate I had no power over them. Every abandonment, whether of a station or a ticket or freight agency, is a matter that is dealt with by the management, and though protests did come from that section of the country, I had no jurisdiction any more than I should have in connection with the Canadian Pacific, if they decided to change some routing or terminus. I would point out to the hon. gentleman, however, that in so far as they had to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners under the existing Railway Act there will be no change in this legislation.

I am sorry to hear the
minister say that because certainly a grave

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
injustice has been done the locality in question, and I was wondering whether the minister would have allowed such a thing to happen.
I had no power to stop it.

We are now dealing with
the economy program, and I want to put this to the minister. Why should twenty-six miles be added to the service between Gaspe and Montreal? The train reaches Matapedia and then runs back eastward over the same ground another thirteen miles.

As the hon. member explains it, it does sound most illogical, and that argument was advanced by those residents of the district who wrote to me. As I usually do in all such matters, I submitted their representations to the management of the Canadian National and they made a reply which I must say was satisfactory to them. I do not say it was satisfactory to me, because I am not competent to pass on the technical side of railway questions; but from their point of view, from the point of view of the economy which would be effected, they claimed that the change was to their advantage. I saw the difficulties which my hon. friend points out, and theTe were also political disadvantages which I should have been glad to have them appreciate, in moving the terminus from one province to another; I knew it would cause considerable difficulty. But they stood by their guns, they maintained that their position was sound, and they explained to me to their own satisfaction that the change was better for them. I had no power to alter their decision.

I would point out to the
minister that the employees were not compensated. The place was simply torn down and Campbellton made the terminal point. A grave injustice has been done not only to the employees but to the locality itself, and I submit that there should be in this legislation or in the Railway Act some provision that would prevent the recurrence of such a change. I know that if the terminus had been removed from Campbellton, New Brunswick, to Matapedia, Quebec, we should have heard from the New Brunswick members; but as a rule we are peaceable and law-abiding in Quebec and we allowed the government to deal with the matter. I impress upon the minister that a grave injustice was done, because the road was built originally with subsidies from Quebec and the terminus was fixed at Matapedia. It remained there for forty years, and suddenly one day the Canadian National Railways step
in and remove the terminus to a point in New Brunswick thirteen miles away, notwithstanding that there is no advantage to be gained from the change; for any railway man will inform the minister that the addition of twenty-six miles, running up and down, morning and night, is an absolute loss which is not compensated by the dismissal of the officials. There is another objection. The train leaves Gaspe and runs two hundred miles through rough country and it must reach Campbellton one hour ahead of the time it reaches Matapedia if it is to connect with the Ocean Limited westbound. If it does not reach Campbellton an hour earlier it cannot connect with the Ocean Limited, and that means that it must leave Gaspe very early in the morning. The result is that the people in that district are put to considerable inconvenience having to take the train at the earlier hour. His Lordship Bishop Ross objected to this and Sir Henry Thornton, when he had the management of the Canadian National Railways, fixed the departure of the train from Gaspe at eight o'clock in order to have it meet the Ocean Limited westbound at Matapedia.
Let me point out to the minister that the Gaspe railway is the best feeder which the Canadian National Railways have east of Montreal. This has been conceded. When Sir Henry Thornton went away the change was made and now the train reaches Campbellton too late. Fresh fish in the fishing season and general merchandise are consequently held up for twenty-four hours. As I say, there is no advantage whatever from the change but on the contrary an additional mileage of twenty-six miles. The passenger has to get off at Matapedia and wait an hour or an hour and a half or run up to Campbellton, covering a distance of thirteen miles each way. I repeat, this is a grave injustice to that section of the country, and I think the minister should amend the act to provide that in the future no such radical change shall be made before the people of the locality are heard by the board.

has not reached the age of sixty-five. When this matter was being discussed before the minister said he would take it under consideration,

I am afraid I cannot suggest a solution of this problem at the moment. It is something which the management will have to take into account when dealing with pension arrangements. That is an arrangement which has been altered at times by the railways and it dates back to the old days of the Grand Trunk. There are at present three systems of pensions, the Grand Trunk railway provident fund, the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway employees' provident fund and the present Canadian National pension plan. I believe it is the intention of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific officials to deal with all pension matters as affecting railway employees. I understand that the railway employees themselves have suggested that the pension schemes be made contributory. I have no doubt that when these matters are being considered, the men's unions will see that they are not lost sight of.

I hope the minister means that he will recommend to whatever tribunal is dealing with this matter allowance of pensions to those who have been deprived of their positions before reaching the age of sixty-five years.	.
Speaking from memory and not wanting to be too definite, I understand that where a man has been working for the company for fifteen years, he is entitled to pension when retired.

I happen to have the
pension regulations before me and I should be very glad if the minister would point out that provision. I should like to quote from the rules and regulations which were passed 
under the provisions of the Canadian National Railways Pension Act, chapter 4, 19-20, George V (1929). Section 8 reads as follows:
Subject to confirmation as provided in rule 4, such pension may be granted by the pension committee to employees on their retirement from the company's service in the following cases:-
(a)	To an employee retiring at the age of 65 years or over, with 15 or more years of service to his credit.
In that case he has to be sixty-five years or over.

(c)	To an employee who, after 10 or more years of service to his credit, becomes incapable of continuing his service by reason of injuries received whilst actually at work in the employment of the company, but only for so long as his incapacity shall continue.
(d)	To an employee of the age of 50 years and upwards with 15 or more years of service to his credit who is discharged from the company's service otherwise than for misconduct.
That covers the point I was making.

If he is fifty years and upwards and is discharged from the company's service otherwise than for misconduct. There would be a very few who would come under that clause after having been in the employ of the company for forty years; they would have to have started work at a very early age.

If the minister will not give me one hundred per cent of what I ask, he might give me a small portion. He seems to be in rather a generous mood this afternoon, and I would ask him to take into serious consideration, not simply throw the suggestion into the waste paper basket, the enactment of a provision that will give to these men compensation even to a limited degree, especially when they have put their life savings into a home in some railway town and find not only their work gone but the value of their property wiped out; because when lines are abandoned, either wholly or in part, the value of the property disappears. I appeal to the minister to include in this act or in an amendment to the Railway Act a provision if not to compensate the men for losing their jobs, at least that they shall receive some compensation for the property they may lose.

Let me put it to the minister in another way. First let me ask him, does he intend to deprive the railroad men of the rights which they now have under section 179 of the Railway Act? I take it that the minister would immediately say no, and ^ I see he nods his head. What I fear is this, now that we are putting all these things back under the railway commission. I fear that the government unintentionally is taking away the privileges which the employees now have. I do not want to go into another lengthy discussion on this thing. I feel that I am making a fair and reasonable appeal to the minister. If there is any delay I am willing to take the blame for it on the ground that I have not been able to make myself understood, but the more I look into it the more plainly I see that when you mention only part of section 179 of the Railway Act, then by inference you say that the other
part of section 179 is inconsistent with the provisions of this act. Although section 179 does not satisfy me, as the minister knows by now, I think that the least we can do in order to preserve for the employees the protection which they now have, and not take anything away from them, is to include the whole of section 179.

I do not wish to go into a lot of detail. The reason I object to section 179 going in in toto is that it refers to section 178. The beginning of section 179 has nothing to do with the employees. Reference is made in section 179 to section 178, and 178 deals with such matters as deviations, changes and alterations; plan, profile, and so forth; sanction; the depositing of plan, profile and book of reference; it provides that the company may execute works, and that the board may dispense with proceedings. A lot of matters are dealt with in section 178, to which section 179 refers, which have nothing whatever to do with the employees of the railway.
I take it that the attitude of the hon. gentleman is to protect the interests of the employees. I submit-I shall not repeat it again whether we vote on this or not-that that part of section 179 which is included in this bill protects the employees so far as they can be protected under section 179. If you put in the whole section you deal with a lot of matters that would interefere to a certain extent with cooperation, and would have no effect on the employees at all but would only complicate matters. If his contention is right, then because we mention the Maritime Freight Rates Act, all other acts must be out of court. That cannot be right because this act prevails over any other act except where the provisions of this act are inconsistent with the provisions of some other act.
I do not intend to argue the matter any further. The hon. gentleman has put himself on record, and certainly I have. With all due respect, and I say this with no disrespect whatsoever for my hon. friend, I prefer to take the opinion of the Justice department and of my own legal advisers as to the interpretation of the act rather than the word of my hon. friend. I must accept the word of the Justice department and of my legal advisers because neither my friend nor I is a lawyer.

Just before the adjournment I was making an appeal to the minister on behalf of those railway men who are likely to lose their homes, which no doubt they have worked a great many yeans to acquire. As regards section 179 of the Railway Act, I do not think it is important whether that provision goes into this legislation because in my opinion the men would still come under the Railway Act. But the important part is the effect which in past years the actual operation of section 179 has had; it has given very little satisfaction to the men affected, and its interpretation, as respects the Big Valley situation, for example, which was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Red Deer, simply meant that although the men had lived in the town for many years and had bought homes, they found, when the time came for a change to be made in connection with that divisional point, that they were entitled to nothing in the way of compensation for their removal. It seems to me it is not a question whether section 179 is incorporated in this legislation; the important point is that the
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

spirit and intent of that section shall be observed in the operation of the bill now before us when it becomes law.
I think it will be generally agreed that in consequence of this bill many hundreds and even thousands of men who have sunk all their savings into homes in small railway divisional points will probably lose everything they possess. I am now pleading for the small man who has invested his all in a home and is now likely, as a result otf the operation of the legislation now before us, to find himself utterly dispossessed. I submit that we shall have to have an amendment to the Railway Act, either in section 179 or by way of a special clause in the act, to meet this situation, because there will probably be thousands of such cases throughout Canada; men will lose not only their jobs but their life savings. Is the minister not prepared to consider favourably the insertion of a clause which will provide for such men some compensation to be determined by the railway board?

In the first place I should not oare to admit the accuracy of my hon. friend's statement that so many men will find themselves in the position he suggests. I think it would be wiser for us to wait until we have seen some of the effects of the legislation before taking action in this regard. If any injustice is done I do not think there is any member of this house who would wish to see the railway men suffer; I do not think anyone wants to see them suffer injustice in consequence of any act of parliament or of the railway companies. If therefore it should prove that men are being unjustly treated, we shall be in a fair position to deal with the matter as and when such injustice occurs. At that time we could discuss the matter on its merits. If it is found after the act goes into operation that there are just grounds for complaint, the question can be considered next session, if we are all here at that time.
I understand and respect my hon. friend's position in this matter, but the government does not accept the premise he lays down, and we are not anxious to include in the legislation any provisions which may not be necessary.

In the Big Valley affair discussed this afternoon, it was shown that men had been actually moved from one place to another and that through a technicality in the law they were not entitled to compensation; yet parliament took no action; indeed, when the matter was brought to the attention of the committee this year it was turned down and the men could get no redress. However, I am glad the minister makes the 
admission that if one year from now it is found that men have lost their homes through process of this legislation, he will take into consideration the suggestion I am now making.
On its merits.

Yes. But I would remind the minister that it is rather dangerous to leave legislation in such a form as to make retroactive measures necessary. Personally, I would rather have parliament take a proper view of the situation now, to anticipate any difficulties that may arise and to make the necessary provision to take care of them.

When this house passes legislation that has for its object the dismissal of thousands of men, I believe that a responsibility rests on the government of the country at least to make some provision for those who will suffer in consequence. I advanced this argument the other day. This question came up in Great Britain when the different railway systems, one hundred and twenty in number, were consolidated into four large systems. There ample protection was provided for the railway workers. I know that in a young country like this, with such a background as ours, it is difficult for us to appreciate action of that sort. In connection with the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg, take the railway towns in northern Ontario; when a man loses employment there he loses everything, because his home depreciates in value. Such men are more or less cut off from civilization as we know it in the larger centres. There is not the remotest possibility therefore of their receiving anything approaching the value of the property they own. There is really only one thing that they can do, and that is to leave their homes and swell the ranks of the unemployed in the large cities of Ontario.
In its practical application, whether we like it or not, this legidation will throw many railway workers on the streets. We need not deceive ourselves in this matter. In my judgment, no consideration at all was given by the framers of this bill to the human element in the railway industry. Section 179 of the Railway Act is to ail intents and purposes a dead letter in the application of this legislation. An example was cited by the previous speaker. It was necessary in western Canada to shut down a divisional point, and all that had to be done was to leave one crew there and section 179 did not apply.
I believe the responsibility rests upon the government at this time to make some provision for the railway men who are going to

lose their jobs. I do not want to labour the point, but after all these men are making a greater sacrifice than the people who invested in the industry. Surely it is not beyond the wisdom of any government to deal with such a situation. I think it could very well be done before the final passage of this bill, and that would be far better than waiting a year. I appreciate the position of the minister, but it is not a question of waiting to see how the legislation will work, because the displacement of labour through the consolidation of the two railways is an actual problem. It is not beyond the realm of possibility that we shall have amalgamation within eighteen months of the passing of this legislation, and this by sheer force of economics. It seems to me the government could quite easily make provision, small as it might be, to take care of the men, because we might as well sign the death warrant of those who are being laid off in the railway industry as leave the act in its present shape. These men have absolutely no hope of finding employment in any of the centres of the dominion.

What is not so obvious is that, even under the best of conditions, terminals constantly put a brake on the rapidity with which traffic moves and cause irregularities which shippers or receivers of freight find it difficult to contend with. As Mr. Loree has well expressed it, "the large terminal stations and the large terminal yards are the graveyard of cars." His calculations indicate that considerably more than two-thirds of the 14-9 days involved in a typical completed car movement is spent in terminals. If IMr. Young.]
such items as surplus cars, Sunday and holiday delays, and delays due to repairs be eliminated from the calculations, 86 per cent of the time is chargeable to terminal operations and only 14 per cent to the line haul. There has been improvement in recent years, but this has been general and it is doubtful whether the proportions indicated have undergone much change More expeditious and regular movement of freight is. therefore, conditioned very largely by the adequacy of terminal facilities and the effectiveness shown in their use.
I have read that paragraph to impress upon, the committee the importance of terminal facilities. Some years ago the government undertook to improve the terminals at Montreal. Now, as everyone knows, the condition in Montreal, so far as terminals are concerned, was deplorable. In his speech introducing the bill at the time Mr. Dunning pointed out that the Canadian National Railways have in Montreal three different stations, all disconnected. When it was desired to transfer a car from one to the other they had to take it out of the city and around the mountain a distance of eighteen miles in order to bring it to another part of the city. The expense was enormous and the delay considerable, and this perhaps will account for the necessity of ordering new cars. The plan was to spend $50,000,000 in improving the terminals at Montreal, not more than $10,000,000 in any one year. When the present government came in, however, they said, "We cannot afford that expenditure; we will discontinue the development of these terminals." They did so; they laid off men; they saved that $10,000,000 a year which would have been spent in Montreal for that purpose. But what did they do? They turned around and spent $10,000,000 buying new cars.

We did not; the management did, and not at our request either.
Mr, YOUNG: The management bought new cars. Did the management find it necessary to buy new cars because they had not adequate terminal facilities? The government abandoned the project, though it was necessary to the railways and would have given employment to thousands of people, because it was costing $10,000,000 a year; and for some reason or other an additional $10,000.000 was spent on equipment which, according to the Duff report, was not necessary.

I would hope that the minister would see the advantage from a public point of view of inserting just that one clause in that way for that reason.
As I see it, the railway employees to-day are suspicious of this act. They fear that it is going to throw many of them out of employment, and that a lot of them will suffer
