I do not know why the hon. member for Vancouver Centre laughs. I have discussed this bill for three weeks, and I have not brought in politics until tonight. I have discussed it on as high a plane as any man could although 1 have been egged on a number of times by hon. gentlemen to bring in political issues because they have brought them in themselves, not many of them, but one or two. I do not wish to get into political discussions about the matter at all. I simply took the attitude that we did not instruct Sir Henry Thornton, and anyway what has that got to do with the question before us? Sir Henry Thornton was a director of the Royal bank for years under the regime of the right hon. gentleman, and if it was wrong to have a director of the Royal bank or of any other company as president of the Canadian National Railway, why did not the right hon. gentleman stop Sir Henry Thornton from being a director? I am advised that he was a director of other companies. I do not know that I could name them, and I am not saying that to his discredit at all; but if it is wrong now for a trustee to be a director of other companies, it was wrong for Sir Henry Thornton to be a director of the Royal bank under the regime of the right hon. gentleman. I do not know where the consistency comes in.

I wonder if the minister, now that we are talking on the subject of Sir Henry Thornton, would be good enough to tell the house whether he asked Sir Henry Thornton to resign from his position as president of the Canadian National Railways or was he just merely frozen out?

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that it will be for the good of Sir Henry Thornton's memory to discuss him any further than we have already discussed him in this house. It might be wise for both sides of the house to leave him out of the picture. The only reference I made to him, and I did this incidentally only by way of illustration, was to say that he had been a director of the Royal bank. Unfortunately a few heated words led to a few more, but I think it would be well to leave Sir Henry Thornton out of the picture altogether. I am quite agreeable to doing so, but on the other hand, if it is forced upon me, I am quite ready to discuss the matter fully.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I suggest that the committee get back to the clause under consideration.
I think I shall have to get new batteries on my earphones. I did not hear an answer to the question I put.

I wonder if the minister would meet us half way. It may be true that he cannot get a man of high standing who is not acting as a director of other companies. Would he remove the fear some of us have that a trustee or chairman could be appointed who may or could be a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway? Would he not go half way and place in the bill a proviso that the chairman cannot be a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway?

I will not accept that suggestion. To do so would be a reflection upon the intelligence of the government, and I do not intend to do that. Any government with an atom of intelligence would not appoint a director of the Canadian Pacific to act in a high office on the national system.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I beg to move to add
after subclause 2 of clause 4 a new subclause as follows:
(3) The trustees, other than the chairman, first appointed under the provisions of this act shall from time to time during the terms of their appointments devote to performance of the duties of their office their whole or part time as may be determined from time to time by the governor in council, and the salaries to be paid to such trustees for whole and/or part time service shall be fixed at the time of their appointments.

I repeat that the amendment does not mean a blessed thing, except that the governor in council may or may not employ trustees whole or part time for the first two or three years of their appointment. It does not mean anything. My hon. friend is moving for full time employment during the tenure of their office. Without referring to the discussion which has taken place may I say that the gentleman who undertakes to manage this business will undoubtedly have to be a full time employee. AVe are now substituting a very small board of trustees for a large board of directors. Per-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
sonally I object to the iterm "trustees"; I do not like it. I do not like the suggestion that these gentlemen are managing a bankrupt institution; that is the only implication which can be placed upon the term. However, the government is determined to call them trustees, and that there shall be three on the board. This reference to the fact that they may or may not for the first year or two of their appointments devote their full time to the management of the board appears to me as so much eyewash. I want the governor in council, or the government through the governor in council, to take full responsibility for the appointment and control of these gentlemen, and also to have power to discharge them; otherwise we shall have a board of three gentlemen with power to spend the money of this country. The minister has pointed out that because we have to vote the annual deficits on operations, the income account and such capital accounts as the trustees deem wise to expend, we will have control. We will have no control whatever. We are just handing over to the appointees of this or any other government complete control of the biggest institution in Canada. Then we are binding ourselves to vote money to those gentlemen to spend willy-nilly, as they see fit, in the operation of the road. True, as outlined in the minister's amendments of to-day, there will be some control in connection with the disposal of property. I believe that this is a step in the right direction, and so far as I am concerned it is quite satisfactory. But if the government refuses to take the responsibility for hiring and firing these trustees they are going to fasten a serious handicap upon this road, this national enterprise and the biggest business in Canada to-day. They are divesting themselves of authority which they should retain, and which rightfully belongs to them, and are passing it over to three gentlemen whom they will select but whose actions they will not be able to control one year after they are appointed. Then, except by vote of the House of Commons and Senate combined, the government will be helpless. Why refer this matter to the Senate? We do not refer to the Senate financial matters in connection with the operation of the road. No accounts are referred to that body; they pass them as a matter of course, but they can do nothing with them. But here are three men who are going to spend sums of money as large as this government are spending. The government finds it necessary to have eight or ten ministers to
administer the affairs of the country,, and yet the trustees will be responsible for expenditures comparable to the expenditures by the government.
The government are tying their hands; they are handing money to the trustees, willy-nilly, without any control except the right of the House of Commons and the Senate to dismiss. I believe I do not use language too strong when I say it is ridioulous, and of the many ridiculous things this government has done this is the crowning event. So far as I am concerned, I will oppose the measure as vigorously as I can.

Speaking on the second reading of the bill I stated it was my opinion that the three trustees should give full time to their work. Their task is so colossal that it seems to me there is plenty of work to which each of the three trustees could give his full time. I am pleased that the government has offered an amendment which at least in part meets that difficulty. I rise to say however that since the government recognizes the necessity for full time employment of the three trustees, upon that should follow when we come to another clause an amendment to the effect that if the three trustees give all their time to the work of their respective offices the chairman alone should not have the complete say as to any action which could be taken by the board of trustees, and that the majority should rule. If the three men give all their time it seems to me it follows that the majority vote should govern the proceedings of the board.
We will deal with that matter later.

I believe the two matters are related. I can see that if two men gave only a small fraction of their time practically all the work of the board of trustees would be done by the chairman. For my part if the two men gave only part of their time, we might as well have one general manager, and be done with it. But if the full board are on full time the majority should govern.

May I repeat that the
expectation of the government at the moment is that they will give their full time to begin with at any rate. As far as I know at the moment that is what probably will be done. But there are reasons why we do not wish that it should be mandatory that the three must be full time. There is in addition the question of salary; it had to be rearranged

C.N.R.-CJP.R. Bill
because of that. I think if the committee will permit the governor in council to take that responsibility, in all probability when the appointments are made the three .men will be for full time to begin with at any rate.

There is another amendment I moved which is closely connected with the amendment we are now considering, namely, as to giving equality of voting power to the three trustees. That is an amendment to section 11, subsection 2.
That is what I was referring to.	[DOT]

If the trustees have the
full voting power I think it gives them a standing. But since this discussion arose it has occurred to me that perhaps we should discuss the two together, if the minister would not object.

We have got only one
clause through, and we have spent days on this bill. I should like to get section 4 through. The point the hon. gentleman raises comes up under section 11. The hon. member for North Waterloo took the same attitude; he thought it was fair to discuss the clauses as we come to them. We are giving in to the hon. gentleman; we will probably do as he suggests in regard to full time, although we are leaving it open. Having done that let us dispose of clause 4.

Perhaps it would be
better to leave this until we consider section 11, because I may say very frankly that after being rather disposed to appreciate what was being done as a step in the right direction, I now feel that if the minister still intends to handicap the trustees by not allowing them to carry -any resolution except with the vote of the chairman, this does not help us at all.

The minister was kind enough to let me see a copy of 'the amendment proposed. I would like to ask him to explain why he requires the words "from time to time" in it. As it reads now the trustees other than the chairman shall devote whole or part time. I should imagine that that would be sufficient, whole or part time as determined by the governor in council. But he adds, "as may be determined from time to time by the governor in council."

I have had the opinion
of a number of outstanding railway men that they did not think the men should be full

time appointments. It is possible that three full time men might be a case of too many cooks spoiling the broth; it might not be satisfactory for the railway. The reason the amendment is drawn in what may appear to be somewhat loose terms is to give power to the governor in council to alter it if the matter did not work out as hoped. It is not put in for any other purpose, except that and the question of salary. I do not want to go over that again, but the salary question comes in in section 7. If we should carry that section we could not change their salaries without an address of the Senate and the House of Commons, or new legislation. Therefore this clause was drawn by the Justice department and my legal officers with the object of giving the governor in council some power in the matter.
I wish the minister had drawn it himself. I think he could have made it a lot more intelligible.
Carried.

Let this stand until we
deal with section 11 and consider the two together; because this is not satisfactory to me, if it is the intention of the minister that these men will be what I have already described as crippled trustees.

All right. But may I
point out with all respect that my hon. friend and his group are a little difficult to satisfy. We have now brought in at least three important amendments, showing a desire to reach satisfactory agreements between hon. gentlemen opposite and ourselves, and the result after nearly three weeks of discussion is that we have now two sections passed, the name of the bill and section 2. Now my hon. friends ask me to hold up section 4. I am not quarrelling, but I would like to put it on record that hon. gentlemen opposite certainly are not easy to satisfy.

I am as anxious as my
hon. friend to get this matter disposed of in a reasonable time. When we get along to section 11 we will be able to discuss the question of who is reasonable.

I do not think the hon. minister ought to leave on record the statement that we have been three weeks on this bill. It is true that it is three weeks since the bill was introduced, but we have spent only a day or two each week on it.

And it is also true that practically all the clauses are through now with the exception of a few that the minister himself asked to stand.

All the uncontentious
parts are through, but practically none that were contentious. I will admit that three weeks is a slight exaggeration, but it is nearer three than two. On the second reading we took a full week, and took the better part of a week on some clauses.

All the better for the bill.
Progress reported.
